entries.d29cb8a0585d79b9cdf2bb7e291e80ed9d261cee: <div sID="gen2656" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="26" osisID="Lev.26" sID="Lev.26"/> <div eID="gen2656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2657" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2658" type="x-p"/> This chapter is a solemn conclusion of the main body of the levitical law. The precepts that follow in this and the following book either relate to some particular matters or are repetitions and explications of the foregoing institutions. Now this chapter contains a general enforcement of all those laws by promises of reward in case of obedience on the one hand, and threatenings of punishment for disobedience on the other hand, the former to work upon hope, the latter on fear, those two handles of the soul, by which it is taken hold of and managed. Here is, I. A repetition of two or three of the principal of the commandments, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.1-Lev.26.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. An inviting promise of all good things, if they would but keep God's commandments, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.3-Lev.26.13">ver. 3-13</reference>. III. A terrible threatening of ruining judgments which would be brought upon them if they were refractory and disobedient, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.14-Lev.26.39">ver. 14-39</reference>. IV. A gracious promise of the return of mercy to those of them that would repent and reform, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.40-Lev.26.46">ver. 40</reference>, &c. <reference osisRef="Deut.28.1-Deut.28.20">Deut. xxviii</reference> is parallel to this.
entries.30099cad195f7ce5daac3f998ca9a11ecf899fc5: <div eID="gen2658" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2657" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Promises. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2659" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Ye shall make you no idols nor graven image, neither rear you up a standing image, neither shall ye set up <hi type="italic">any</hi> image of stone in your land, to bow down unto it: for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <hi type="super">2</hi> Ye shall keep my sabbaths, and reverence my sanctuary: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">3</hi> If ye walk in my statutes, and keep my commandments, and do them; <hi type="super">4</hi> Then I will give you rain in due season, and the land shall yield her increase, and the trees of the field shall yield their fruit. 5 And your threshing shall reach unto the vintage, and the vintage shall reach unto the sowing time: and ye shall eat your bread to the full, and dwell in your land safely. <hi type="super">6</hi> And I will give peace in the land, and ye shall lie down, and none shall make <hi type="italic">you</hi> afraid: and I will rid evil beasts out of the land, neither shall the sword go through your land. <hi type="super">7</hi> And ye shall chase your enemies, and they shall fall before you by the sword. 8 And five of you shall chase an hundred, and an hundred of you shall put ten thousand to flight: and your enemies shall fall before you by the sword. <hi type="super">9</hi> For I will have respect unto you, and make you fruitful, and multiply you, and establish my covenant with you. <hi type="super">10</hi> And ye shall eat old store, and bring forth the old because of the new. <hi type="super">11</hi> And I will set my tabernacle among you: and my soul shall not abhor you. <hi type="super">12</hi> And I will walk among you, and will be your God, and ye shall be my people. 13 I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, which brought you forth out of the land of Egypt, that ye should not be their bondmen; and I have broken the bands of your yoke, and made you go upright. <div eID="gen2659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2660" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The inculcating of those precepts of the law which were of the greatest consequence, and by which were of the greatest consequence, and by which especially their obedience would be tried, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.1-Lev.26.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. They are the abstract of the second and fourth commandments, which, as they are by much the largest in the decalogue, so they are most frequently insisted on in other parts of the law. As, when a master has given many things in charge to his servant, he concludes with the repetition of those things which were of the greatest importance, and which the servant was most in danger of neglecting, bidding him, whatever he did, be sure to remember those, so here God by Moses, after many precepts, closes all with a special charge to observe these two great commandments. 1. "Be sure you never worship images, nor ever make any sort of images or pictures for a religious use," <reference osisRef="Lev.26.1">v. 1</reference>. No sin was more provoking to God than this, and yet there was none that they were more addicted to, and which afterwards proved of more pernicious consequence to them. Next to God's being, unity, and universal influence, it is necessary that we know and believe that he is an infinite Spirit; and therefore to represent him by an image in the making of it, to confine him to an image in the consecrating of it, and to worship him by an image in bowing down to it, <hi type="italic">changes his truth into a lie</hi> and <hi type="italic">his glory into shame,</hi> as much as any thing. 2. "Be sure you keep up a great veneration for sabbaths and religious assemblies," <reference osisRef="Lev.26.2">v. 2</reference>. As nothing tends more to corrupt religion than the use of images in devotion, so nothing contributes more to the support of it than <hi type="italic">keeping the sabbaths</hi> and <hi type="italic">reverencing the sanctuary.</hi> These make up very much of the instrumental part of religion, by which the essentials of it are kept up. Therefore we find in the prophets that, next to the sin of idolatry, there is no sin for which the Jews are more frequently reproved and threatened than the profanation of the sabbath day. <div eID="gen2660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2661" type="x-p"/> II. Great encouragements given them to live in constant obedience to all God's commandments, largely and strongly assuring them that if they did so they should be a happy people, and should be blessed with all the good things they could desire. Human governments enforce their laws with penalties to be inflicted for the breach of them; but God will be known as <hi type="italic">the rewarder of those that seek and serve him.</hi> Let us take a view of these great and precious promises, which, though they relate chiefly to the life which now is, and to the public national concerns of that people, were typical of the spiritual blessings entailed by the covenant of grace upon all believers through Christ. 1. Plenty and abundance of the fruits of the earth. They should have seasonable rain, neither too little nor too much, but what was requisite for their land, which was watered with the dew of heaven (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.10-Deut.11.11">Deut. xi. 10, 11</reference>), that it might <hi type="italic">yield its increase,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.4">v. 4</reference>. The dependence which the fruitfulness of the earth beneath has upon the influences of heaven above is a sensible intimation to us that every good and perfect gift must be expected <hi type="italic">from above,</hi> from the <hi type="italic">Father of lights.</hi> It is promised that the earth should produce its fruits in such great abundance that they would be kept in full employment, during both the harvest and the vintage, to gather it in, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.5">v. 5</reference>. Before they had reaped their corn and threshed it, the vintage would be ready; and, before they had finished their vintage, it would be high time to begin their sowing. Long harvests are often with us the consequences of bad weather, but with them they should be the effects of a great increase. This signified the abundance of grace which should be poured out in gospel times, when the <hi type="italic">ploughman should overtake the reaper</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.13">Amos ix. 13</reference>), and a great harvest of souls should be gathered in to Christ. The plenty should be so great that they should <hi type="italic">bring forth the old</hi> to be given away to the poor <hi type="italic">because of the new,</hi> to make room for it in their barns, which yet they would not <hi type="italic">pull down to build greater,</hi> as that rich fool (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.18">Luke xii. 18</reference>), for God gave them this abundance to be laid out, not be hoarded up from one year to another. <hi type="italic">He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.11.26">Prov. xi. 26</reference>. That promise (<reference osisRef="Mal.3.10">Mal. iii. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it,</hi> explains this, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.10">v. 10</reference>. And that which crowns this blessing of plenty is (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.5">v. 5</reference>), You shall <hi type="italic">eat your bread to the full,</hi> which intimates that they should have, not only abundance, but content and satisfaction in it. They should have enough, and should know when they had enough. Thus <hi type="italic">the meek shall eat and be satisfied,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.22.26">Ps. xxii. 26</reference>. 2. Peace under the divine protection; "<hi type="italic">You shall dwell in your land safely</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.5">v. 5</reference>); both really save, and safe in your own apprehensions; you shall lie down to rest in the power and promise of God, and not only none shall hurt you, but none shall so much as <hi type="italic">make you afraid,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Lev.26.6">v. 6</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Ps.4.8">Ps. iv. 8</reference>. They should not be infested with wild beasts, these should be <hi type="italic">rid out of the land,</hi> or, as it is promised (<reference osisRef="Job.5.23">Job v. 23</reference>), should <hi type="italic">be at peace with them.</hi> Nor should they be terrified with the alarms of war: <hi type="italic">Neither shall the sword go through your land.</hi> This holy security is promised to all the faithful, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1-Ps.91.16">Ps. xci. 1</reference>, &c. Those must needs dwell in safety that <hi type="italic">dwell in God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.9.18-Job.9.19">Job ix. 18, 19</reference>. 3. Victory and success in their wars abroad, while they had peace and tranquility at home, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.7-Lev.26.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. They are assured that the hand of God should so signally appear with them in their conquests that no disproportion of numbers should make against them: <hi type="italic">Five of you</hi> shall have courage to attack, and strength to <hi type="italic">chase</hi> and defeat, <hi type="italic">a hundred,</hi> as Jonathan did (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.12">1 Sam. xiv. 12</reference>), experiencing the truth of his own maxim (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.6">v. 6</reference>), that it is all one with the Lord to <hi type="italic">save by many or by few.</hi> 4. The increase of their people: <hi type="italic">I will make you fruitful and multiply you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.9">v. 9</reference>. Thus the promise made to Abraham must be fulfilled, that his seed should be <hi type="italic">as the dust of the earth;</hi> and much more numerous they would have been if they had by their sin cut themselves short. It is promised to the gospel church that it shall be fruitful, <reference osisRef="John.15.16">John xv. 16</reference>. 5. The favour of God, which is the fountain of all good: <hi type="italic">I will have respect unto you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.9">v. 9</reference>. If the eye of our faith be unto God, the eye of his favour will be unto us. More is implied than is expressed in that promise, <hi type="italic">My soul shall not abhor you</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.11">v. 11</reference>), as there is in that threatening, <hi type="italic">My soul shall have no pleasure in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.38">Heb. x. 38</reference>. Though there was that among them which might justly have alienated him from them, yet, if they would closely adhere to his institutions, he would not abhor them. 6. Tokens of his presence in and by his ordinances: <hi type="italic">I will set my tabernacle among you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.11">v. 11</reference>. It was their honour and advantage that God's tabernacle was lately erected among them; but here he lets them know that the continuance and establishment of it depended upon their good behaviour. The tabernacle that was now set should be settled if they would be obedient, else not. Note, The way to have God's ordinances fixed among us, as a nail in a sure place, is to cleave closely to the institution of them. It is added (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.12">v. 12</reference>), "<hi type="italic">I will walk among you,</hi> with delight and satisfaction, as a man in his garden; I will keep up communion with you as a man walking with his friend." This seems to be alluded to, <reference osisRef="Rev.2.1">Rev. ii. 1</reference>, where Christ is said to <hi type="italic">walk in the midst of the golden candlesticks.</hi> 7. The grace of the covenant, as the fountain and foundation, the sweetness and security, of all these blessings: <hi type="italic">I will establish my covenant with you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.9">v. 9</reference>. Let them perform their part of the covenant, and God would not fail to perform his. All covenant-blessings are summed up in the covenant-relation (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will be your God, and you shall be my people;</hi> and they are all grounded upon their redemption: <hi type="italic">I am your God,</hi> because <hi type="italic">I brought you forth out of the land of Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.13">v. 13</reference>. Having purchased them, he would own them, and never cast them off till they cast him off. He <hi type="italic">broke their yoke,</hi> and <hi type="italic">made them go upright,</hi> that is, their deliverance out of Egypt put them in a state both of ease and honour, that, being delivered out of the hands of their enemies, they might <hi type="italic">serve God without fear,</hi> each walking <hi type="italic">in his uprightness.</hi> When Israel rejected Christ, and was therefore rejected by him, their back is said to be <hi type="italic">bowed down</hi> always under the burden of their guilt, which was heavier than that of their bondage in Egypt, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.10">Rom. xi. 10</reference>.
entries.15cf1a48dbdb5b3716139ca3d92a4be44f1a92ab: <div eID="gen2661" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Threatenings. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2662" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> But if ye will not hearken unto me, and will not do all these commandments; <hi type="super">15</hi> And if ye shall despise my statutes, or if your soul abhor my judgments, so that ye will not do all my commandments, <hi type="italic">but</hi> that ye break my covenant: 16 I also will do this unto you; I will even appoint over you terror, consumption, and the burning ague, that shall consume the eyes, and cause sorrow of heart: and ye shall sow your seed in vain, for your enemies shall eat it. <hi type="super">17</hi> And I will set my face against you, and ye shall be slain before your enemies: they that hate you shall reign over you; and ye shall flee when none pursueth you. <hi type="super">18</hi> And if ye will not yet for all this hearken unto me, then I will punish you seven times more for your sins. 19 And I will break the pride of your power; and I will make your heaven as iron, and your earth as brass: <hi type="super">20</hi> And your strength shall be spent in vain: for your land shall not yield her increase, neither shall the trees of the land yield their fruits. 21 And if ye walk contrary unto me, and will not hearken unto me; I will bring seven times more plagues upon you according to your sins. <hi type="super">22</hi> I will also send wild beasts among you, which shall rob you of your children, and destroy your cattle, and make you few in number; and your <hi type="italic">high</hi> ways shall be desolate. <hi type="super">23</hi> And if ye will not be reformed by me by these things, but will walk contrary unto me; <hi type="super">24</hi> Then will I also walk contrary unto you, and will punish you yet seven times for your sins. <hi type="super">25</hi> And I will bring a sword upon you, that shall avenge the quarrel of <hi type="italic">my</hi> covenant: and when ye are gathered together within your cities, I will send the pestilence among you; and ye shall be delivered into the hand of the enemy. 26 <hi type="italic">And</hi> when I have broken the staff of your bread, ten women shall bake your bread in one oven, and they shall deliver <hi type="italic">you</hi> your bread again by weight: and ye shall eat, and not be satisfied. <hi type="super">27</hi> And if ye will not for all this hearken unto me, but walk contrary unto me; <hi type="super">28</hi> Then I will walk contrary unto you also in fury; and I, even I, will chastise you seven times for your sins. <hi type="super">29</hi> And ye shall eat the flesh of your sons, and the flesh of your daughters shall ye eat. <hi type="super">30</hi> And I will destroy your high places, and cut down your images, and cast your carcases upon the carcases of your idols, and my soul shall abhor you. <hi type="super">31</hi> And I will make your cities waste, and bring your sanctuaries unto desolation, and I will not smell the savour of your sweet odours. <hi type="super">32</hi> And I will bring the land into desolation: and your enemies which dwell therein shall be astonished at it. <hi type="super">33</hi> And I will scatter you among the heathen, and will draw out a sword after you: and your land shall be desolate, and your cities waste. <hi type="super">34</hi> Then shall the land enjoy her sabbaths, as long as it lieth desolate, and ye <hi type="italic">be</hi> in your enemies' land; <hi type="italic">even</hi> then shall the land rest, and enjoy her sabbaths. <hi type="super">35</hi> As long as it lieth desolate it shall rest; because it did not rest in your sabbaths, when ye dwelt upon it. <hi type="super">36</hi> And upon them that are left <hi type="italic">alive</hi> of you I will send a faintness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies; and the sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them; and they shall flee, as fleeing from a sword; and they shall fall when none pursueth. <hi type="super">37</hi> And they shall fall one upon another, as it were before a sword, when none pursueth: and ye shall have no power to stand before your enemies. <hi type="super">38</hi> And ye shall perish among the heathen, and the land of your enemies shall eat you up. <hi type="super">39</hi> And they that are left of you shall pine away in their iniquity in your enemies' lands; and also in the iniquities of their fathers shall they pine away with them. <div eID="gen2662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2663" type="x-p"/> After God had set the blessing before them (the life and good which would make them a happy people if they would be obedient), he here sets the curse before them, the death and evil which would make them as miserable if they were disobedient. Let them not think themselves so deeply rooted as that God's power could not ruin them, nor so highly favoured as that his justice would not ruin them if they revolted from him and rebelled against him; no <hi type="italic">You only have I known, therefore I will punish you</hi> soonest and sorest. <reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Amos iii. 2</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen2663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2664" type="x-p"/> I. How their sin is described, which would bring all this misery upon them. Not sins of ignorance and infirmity; God had provided sacrifices for those. Not the sins they repented of and forsook; but the sins that were presumptuously committed, and obstinately persisted in. Two things would certainly bring this ruin upon them:— <div eID="gen2664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2665" type="x-p"/> 1. A contempt of God's commandments (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.14">v. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If you will not hearken to me</hi> speaking to you by the law, nor <hi type="italic">do all these commandments,</hi> that is, desire and endeavour to do them, and, wherein you miss it, make use of the prescribed remedies." Thus their sin is supposed to begin in mere carelessness, and neglect, and omission. These are bad enough, but they make way for worse; for the people are brought in (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.15">v. 15</reference>) as, (1.) <hi type="italic">Despising God's statutes,</hi> both the duties enjoined and the authority enjoining them, thinking meanly of the law and the Law-maker. Note, Those are hastening apace to their own ruin who begin to think it below them to be religious. (2.) <hi type="italic">Abhorring his judgments,</hi> their very souls abhorring them. Note, Those that begin to despise religion will come by degrees to loathe it; and mean thoughts of it will ripen into ill thoughts of it; those that turn from it will turn against it, and their hearts will rise at it. (3.) <hi type="italic">Breaking his covenant.</hi> Though every breach of the commandment does not amount to a breach of the covenant (we were undone if it did), yet, when men have come to such a pitch of impiety as to despise and abhor the commandment, the next step will be to disown God, and all relation to him. Those that reject the precept will come at last to renounce the covenant. Observe, It is God's covenant which they break: he made it, but they break it. Note, If a covenant be made and kept between God and man, God must have all the honour; but, if ever it be broken, man must bear all the blame: on him shall this breach be. <div eID="gen2665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2666" type="x-p"/> 2. A contempt of his corrections. Even their disobedience would not have been their destruction if they had not been obstinate and impenitent in it, notwithstanding the methods God took to reclaim them. Their contempt of God's word would not have brought them to ruin, if they had not added to that a contempt of his rod, which should have brought them to repentance. Three ways this is expressed:—(1.) "<hi type="italic">If you will not for all this hearken to me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.18">v. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.21">21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.27">27</reference>. If you will not learn obedience by the things which you suffer, but be as deaf to the loud alarms of God's judgments as you have been to the close reasonings of his word and the secret whispers of your own consciences, you are obstinate indeed." (2.) "<hi type="italic">If you walk contrary to me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.21">v. 21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.23">23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.27">27</reference>. All sinners walk contrary to God, to his truths, laws, and counsels; but those especially that are incorrigible under his judgments. The design of the rod is to humble them, and soften them, and bring them to repentance; but, instead of this, their hearts are more hardened and exasperated against God, and <hi type="italic">in their distress</hi> they <hi type="italic">trespass yet more against him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.22">2 Chron. xxviii. 22</reference>. This is walking contrary to God. Some read it, "If you walk at all adventures with me, carelessly and presumptuously, as if you heeded not either what you do, whether it be right or wrong, or what God does with you, whether it be for you or against you, blundering on in wilful ignorance." (3.) <hi type="italic">If you will not be reformed by these things.</hi> God's design in punishing is to reform, by giving men sensible convictions of the evil of sin, and obliging them to seek unto him for relief: this is the primary intention; but those that will not be reformed by the judgments of God must expect to be ruined by them. Those have a great deal to answer for that have been long and often under God's correcting hand, and yet go on frowardly in a sinful way; sick and in pain, and yet not reformed; crossed and impoverished, and yet not reformed; broken with breach upon breach, yet <hi type="italic">not returning to the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.4.6">Amos iv. 6</reference>, &c. <div eID="gen2666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2667" type="x-p"/> II. How the misery is described which their sin would bring upon them, under two heads:— <div eID="gen2667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2668" type="x-p"/> 1. God himself would be against them; and this is the root and cause of all their misery. (1.) <hi type="italic">I will set my face against you</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.17">v. 17</reference>), that is, "I will set myself against you, set myself to ruin you." These proud sinners God will resist, and face those down that confront his authority. Or the face is put for the anger: "I will show myself highly displeased at you." (2.) <hi type="italic">I will walk contrary to you</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.24">v. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.28">28</reference>); <hi type="italic">with the forward he will wrestle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.28.26">Ps. xxviii. 26</reference> [margin]. When God in his providence thwarts the designs of a people, which they thought well laid, crosses their purposes, breaks their measures, blasts their endeavours, and disappoints their expectations, then he walks contrary to them. Note, There is nothing got by striving with God Almighty, for he will break either the heart or the neck of those that contend with him, will bring them either to repentance or ruin. "I will walk at all adventures with you," so some read; "all covenant loving-kindness shall be forgotten, and I will leave you to common providence." Note, Those that cast off God deserve that he should cast them off. (3.) As they continued obstinate, the judgments should increase yet more upon them. If the first sensible tokens of God's displeasures do not attain their end, to humble and reform them, then (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.18">v. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will punish you seven times more,</hi> and again (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.21">v. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will bring seven times more plagues,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.24">v. 24</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will punish you yet seven times,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.28">v. 28</reference>), <hi type="italic">I, even I, will chastise you seven times for your sins.</hi> Note, If less judgments do not do their work, God will send greater; for, when he <hi type="italic">judges, he will overcome.</hi> If true repentance do not stay process, it will go on till execution be taken out. Those that are obstinate and incorrigible, when they have weathered one storm must expect another more violent; and, how severely soever they are punished, till they are in hell they must still say, "There is worse behind," unless they repent. If the <hi type="italic">founder have</hi> hitherto <hi type="italic">melted in vain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.29">Jer. vi. 29</reference>), the furnace will be heated <hi type="italic">seven times hotter</hi> (a proverbial expression, used <reference osisRef="Dan.3.19">Dan. iii. 19</reference>), and again and again <hi type="italic">seven times hotter;</hi> and who among us can dwell with such devouring fire? God does not begin with the sorest judgments, to show that he is patient, and delights not in the death of sinners; but, if they repent not, he will proceed to the sorest, to show that he is righteous, and that he will not be mocked or set at defiance. (4.) Their misery is completed in that threatening: <hi type="italic">My soul shall abhor you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">v. 30</reference>. That man is as miserable as he can be whom God abhors; for his resentments are just and effective. Thus <hi type="italic">if any man draw back,</hi> as these are supposed to do, <hi type="italic">God's soul shall have no pleasure in him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.38">Heb. x. 38</reference>), and he will <hi type="italic">spue them out of his mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.16">Rev. iii. 16</reference>. It is spoken of as strange, and yet too true, <hi type="italic">Hath thy soul loathed Zion?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.14.19">Jer. xiv. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen2668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2669" type="x-p"/> 2. The whole creation would be at war with them. All God's sore judgments would be sent against them; for he hath many arrows in his quiver. The threatenings here are very particular, because really they were prophecies, and he that foresaw all their rebellions knew they would prove so; see <reference osisRef="Deut.31.16">Deut. xxxi. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.29">29</reference>. This long roll of threatening shows that evil pursues sinners. We have here, <div eID="gen2669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2670" type="x-p"/> (1.) Temporal judgments threatened. [1.] Diseases of body, which should be epidemical: <hi type="italic">I will appoint over you,</hi> as task-masters, to rule you with rigour, <hi type="italic">terror, consumption, and the burning ague,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.16">v. 16</reference>. What we translate <hi type="italic">terror,</hi> some think, signifies a particular disease, probably (says the learned bishop Patrick) the <hi type="italic">falling sickness,</hi> which is terror indeed: all chronical diseases are included in the consumption, and all acute diseases in the burning ague or fever. These consume the eyes, and cause sorrow both to those that are visited with them and to their friends and relations. Note, All diseases are God's servants; they do what he appoints them, and are often used as scourges wherewith he chastises a provoking people. The pestilence is threatened (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.25">v. 25</reference>) to meet them, when they are gathered together in their cities for fear of the sword. The greater the concourse of people is, the greater desolation does the pestilence make; and, when it gets among the soldiers that should defend a place, it is of most fatal consequence. [2.] Famine and scarcity of bread, which should be brought upon them several ways; as, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> By plunder (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">Your enemies shall eat it</hi> up, and carry it off as the Midianites did, <reference osisRef="Judg.6.5-Judg.6.6">Judg. vi. 5, 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> By unseasonable weather, especially the want of rain (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will make your heaven as iron,</hi> letting fall no rain, but reflecting heat, and then the earth would of course be as dry and hard <hi type="italic">as brass,</hi> and their labour in ploughing and sowing would <hi type="italic">be in vain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.20">v. 20</reference>); for the increase of the earth depends upon God's good providence more than upon man's good husbandry. This should be the breaking of the <hi type="italic">staff of bread</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.26">v. 26</reference>), which life leans upon, and is supported by, on which perhaps they had leaned more than upon God's blessing. There should be so great a dearth of corn that, whereas every family used to fill an oven of their own with household bread, now ten families should have to fill but one over, which would bring themselves and their children and servants to short allowance, so that they should <hi type="italic">eat and not be satisfied.</hi> The less they had the more craving should their appetites be. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> By the besieging of their cities, which would reduce them to such an extremity that they should <hi type="italic">eat the flesh of their sons and daughters,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.29">v. 29</reference>. [3.] War, and the prevailing of their enemies over them: "<hi type="italic">You shall be slain before your enemies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.17">v. 17</reference>. Your choice men shall die in battle, and <hi type="italic">those that hate you shall reign over you,</hi> and justly, since you are not willing that the God that loved you should reign over you;" <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.8">2 Chron. xii. 8</reference>. Miserable is that people whose enemies are their rulers and have got dominion over them, or whose rulers have become their enemies and under-hand seek the ruin of their interests. Thus God would <hi type="italic">break the pride of their power,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.19">v. 19</reference>. God had given them power over the nations; but when they, instead of being thankful for that power, and improving it for the service of God's kingdom, grew proud of it, and perverted the intentions of it, it was just with God to break it. Thus God would <hi type="italic">bring a sword upon them to avenge the quarrel of his covenant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.25">v. 25</reference>. Note, God has a just quarrel with those that break covenant with him, for he will not be mocked by the treachery of perfidious men; and one way or other he will avenge this quarrel upon those that play at fast and loose with him. [4.] Wild beasts, lions, bears, and wolves, which should increase upon them, and tear in pieces all that come in their way (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.22">v. 22</reference>), as we read of two bears that in an instant killed forty-two children, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.24">2 Kings ii. 24</reference>. This is one of the four sore judgments threatened <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.21">Ezek. xiv. 21</reference>, which plainly refers to this chapter. Man was made to have dominion over the creatures, and, though many of them are stronger than he, yet none of them could have hurt him, nay, all of them would have served him, if he had not first shaken off God's dominion, and so lost his own; and now the creatures are in rebellion against him that is in rebellion against his Maker, and, when the Lord of those hosts pleases, they are the executioners of his wrath and the ministers of his justice. [5.] Captivity, or dispersion: <hi type="italic">I will scatter you among the heathen</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.33">v. 33</reference>), <hi type="italic">in your enemies' land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.34">v. 34</reference>. Never were any people so incorporated and united among themselves as they were; but for their sin God would scatter them, so that they should be lost among the heathen, from whom God had graciously distinguished them, but with whom they had wickedly mingled themselves. Yet, when they were scattered, divine justice had not done with them, but would draw out a sword after them, which would find them out, and follow them wherever they were. God's judgments, as they cannot be outfaced, so they cannot be outrun. [6.] The utter ruin and desolation of their land, which should be so remarkable that their very enemies themselves, who had helped it forward, should in the review be astonished at it, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.32">v. 32</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Their cities should be waste, forsaken, uninhabited, and all the buildings destroyed; those that escaped the desolations of war should fall to decay of themselves. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Their sanctuaries should be a desolation, that is, their synagogues where they met for religious worship every sabbath, as well as their tabernacle where they met thrice a year. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The country itself should be desolate, not tilled or husbanded (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.34-Lev.26.35">v. 34, 35</reference>); then the land should enjoy its sabbaths, because they had not religiously observed the sabbatical years which God appointed them. They tilled their ground when God would have them let it rest; justly therefore were they driven out of it; and the expression intimates that the ground itself was pleased and easy when it was rid of the burden of such sinners, under which it had groaned, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.20">Rom. viii. 20</reference>, &c. The captivity in Babylon lasted seventy years, and so long the land <hi type="italic">enjoyed her sabbaths,</hi> as is said (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.21">2 Chron. xxxvi. 21</reference>) with reference to this. [7.] The destruction of their idols, though rather a mercy than a judgment, yet, being a necessary piece of justice, is here mentioned, to show what would be the sin that would bring all these miseries upon them: <hi type="italic">I will destroy your high places,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">v. 30</reference>. Those that will not be parted from their sins by the commands of God shall be parted from them by his judgments; since they would not destroy their high places, God would. And, to upbraid them with the unreasonable fondness they had shown for their idols, it is foretold that their <hi type="italic">carcases should be cast upon the carcases of their idols.</hi> Those that are wedded to their lusts will sooner or later have enough of them. Their idols would not be able to help either themselves or their worshippers; but, those that made them being like them, they should both perish alike, and fall together as blind into the ditch. <div eID="gen2670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2671" type="x-p"/> (2.) Spiritual judgments are here threatened. These should seize the mind; for he that made the mind can, when he pleases, make his sword approach to it. It is here threatened, [1.] That they should find no acceptance with God: <hi type="italic">I will not smell the savour of your sweet odours,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.31">v. 31</reference>. Though the judgments of God upon them did not separate them and their sins, yet they extorted incense from them; but in vain—even their incense was an abomination, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.13">Isa. i. 13</reference>. [2.] That they should have no courage in their wars, but should be quite dispirited and disheartened. They should not only fear and flee (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.17">v. 17</reference>), but fear and <hi type="italic">fall, when none pursued,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.36">v. 36</reference>. A guilty conscience would be their continual terror, so that not only the sound of a trumpet, but the very <hi type="italic">sound of a leaf, should chase them.</hi> Note, Those that cast off the fear of God expose themselves to the fear of every thing else, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.1">Prov. xxviii. 1</reference>. Their very fears should dash them <hi type="italic">one against another,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.37-Lev.26.38">v. 37, 38</reference>. And those that had increased one another's guilt would now increase one another's fears. [3.] That they should have no hope of the forgiveness of their sins (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.39">v. 39</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall pine away in their iniquity,</hi> and <hi type="italic">how should they then live?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.10">Ezek. xxxiii. 10</reference>. Note, It is a righteous thing with God to leave those to despair of pardon that have presumed to sin; and it is owing to free grace if we are not abandoned to pine away in the iniquity we were born in and have lived in.
entries.d691fda7d257a5ae4a24526b4753cea3b474272c: <div eID="gen2671" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Threatenings and Promises. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2672" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">40</hi> If they shall confess their iniquity, and the iniquity of their fathers, with their trespass which they trespassed against me, and that also they have walked contrary unto me; <hi type="super">41</hi> And <hi type="italic">that</hi> I also have walked contrary unto them, and have brought them into the land of their enemies; if then their uncircumcised hearts be humbled, and they then accept of the punishment of their iniquity: <hi type="super">42</hi> Then will I remember my covenant with Jacob, and also my covenant with Isaac, and also my covenant with Abraham will I remember; and I will remember the land. <hi type="super">43</hi> The land also shall be left of them, and shall enjoy her sabbaths, while she lieth desolate without them: and they shall accept of the punishment of their iniquity: because, even because they despised my judgments, and because their soul abhorred my statutes. <hi type="super">44</hi> And yet for all that, when they be in the land of their enemies, I will not cast them away, neither will I abhor them, to destroy them utterly, and to break my covenant with them: for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God. <hi type="super">45</hi> But I will for their sakes remember the covenant of their ancestors, whom I brought forth out of the land of Egypt in the sight of the heathen, that I might be their God: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">46</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the statutes and judgments and laws, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> made between him and the children of Israel in Mount Sinai by the hand of Moses. <div eID="gen2672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2673" type="x-p"/> Here the chapter concludes with gracious promises of the return of God's favour to them upon their repentance, that they might not (unless it were their own fault) <hi type="italic">pine away in their iniquity.</hi> Behold, with wonder, the riches of God's mercy to a people that had obstinately stood it out against the judgments of God, and would never think of surrendering till they were reduced to the last extremity. Yet <hi type="italic">turn to strong-hold, you prisoners of hope,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.9.12">Zech. ix. 12</reference>. As bad as things are, they may be mended. <hi type="italic">Yet there is hope in Israel.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen2673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2674" type="x-p"/> I. How the repentance which would qualify them for this mercy is described, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.40-Lev.26.41">v. 40, 41</reference>. The instances of it are three:—1. Confession, by which they must give glory to God, and take shame to themselves. There must be a confession of sin, their own and their fathers', which they must lament the guilt of because they feel the smart of it; that thus they may cut off the entail of wrath. They must in their confession put sin under its worst character, as <hi type="italic">walking contrary to God;</hi> this is the sinfulness of sin, the worst thing in it, and which in our repentance we should especially bewail. There must also be a confession of wrath; they must overlook the instruments of their trouble and the second causes, and confess that God has <hi type="italic">walked contrary to them,</hi> and so <hi type="italic">dealt with them according to their sins.</hi> Such a confession as this we find made by Daniel just before the dawning of the day of their deliverance (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.1-Dan.9.27">ch. ix.</reference>), and the like, <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.1-Ezra.9.15">Ezra ix.</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.9.2">Neh. ix. 2</reference>. Remorse and godly sorrow for sin: <hi type="italic">If their uncircumcised heart be humbled.</hi> An impenitent, unbelieving, unhumbled heart, is called an <hi type="italic">uncircumcised</hi> heart, the heart of a Gentile that is a stranger to God, rather than the heart of an Israelite in covenant with him. True circumcision is <hi type="italic">of the heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.29">Rom. ii. 29</reference>), without which the circumcision of the flesh avails nothing, <reference osisRef="Jer.9.26">Jer. ix. 26</reference>. Now in repentance this uncircumcised heart was humbled, that is, it was truly broken and contrite for sin. Note, A humble heart under humbling providences prepares for deliverance and true comfort. 3. Submission to the justice of God in all his dealings; if they then <hi type="italic">accept of the punishment of their iniquity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.41">v. 41</reference> and again <reference osisRef="Lev.26.43">v. 43</reference>), that is, if they justify God and condemn themselves, patiently bear the punishment as that which they have well deserved, and carefully answer the ends of it as that which God has well designed, accept it as a kindness, take it as physic, and improve it, then they are penitents indeed. <div eID="gen2674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2675" type="x-p"/> II. How the mercy which they should obtain upon their repentance is described. 1. They should not be abandoned: <hi type="italic">Though they have despised my judgments, yet, for all that, I will not cast them away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.43-Lev.26.44">v. 43, 44</reference>. He speaks as a tender Father that cannot find in his heart to disinherit a son that has been very provoking. <hi type="italic">How shall I do it?</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.11.8-Hos.11.9">Hos. xi. 8, 9</reference>. Till he had laid the foundations of a church for himself in the Gentile world, the Jewish church was not quite forsaken, nor cast away. 2. They should be remembered: <hi type="italic">I will remember the land</hi> with favour, which is grounded upon the promise before, <hi type="italic">I will remember my covenant</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.42">v. 42</reference>), which is repeated, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.45">v. 45</reference>. God is said <hi type="italic">to remember the covenant</hi> when he performs the promises of it, purely for his faithfulness' sake; not because there is any thing in us to recommend us to his favour, but because he will be as good as his word. This is the church's plea. <reference osisRef="Ps.74.20">Ps. lxxiv. 20</reference>, <hi type="italic">Have respect unto the covenant.</hi> He will remember the constitution of the covenant, which is such as leaves room for repentance, and promises pardon upon repentance; and the Mediator of the covenant, who was promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and was sent, when the fulness of time came, in remembrance of that holy covenant. The word covenant is thrice repeated, to intimate that God is ever mindful of it and would have us to be so. The persons also with whom the covenant was made are mentioned in an unusual manner, <hi type="italic">per modum ascensus—in the ascending line,</hi> beginning with Jacob, to lead them gradually to the most ancient promise, which was made to the father of the faithful: thus (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.20">Mic. vii. 20</reference>) he is said to perform the <hi type="italic">truth to Jacob,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">mercy to Abraham.</hi> He will for their sakes (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.45">v. 45</reference>), not their merit's sake, but their benefit's sake, remember the covenant of their ancestors, and upon that score show kindness to them, though most unworthy; they are therefore said to be, <hi type="italic">as touching the election, beloved for the fathers' sake,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.28">Rom. xi. 28</reference>. Note, When those that have walked contrary to God in a way of sin return to him by sincere repentance, though he has walked contrary to them in a way of judgment he will return to them in a way of special mercy, pursuant to the covenant of redemption and grace. None are so ready to repent as God is to forgive upon repentance, through Christ, who is given for a covenant. <div eID="gen2675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2676" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> These are said to be <hi type="italic">the laws which the Lord made between him and the children of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.46">v. 46</reference>. His communion with his church is kept up by his law. He manifests not only his dominion over them, but his favour to them, by giving them his law; and they manifest not only their holy fear, but their holy love, by the observance of it; and thus it is made between them, rather as a covenant than a law; for he draws with the cords of a man.  <chapter eID="Lev.26"/> <div eID="gen2676" type="x-p"/>

entries.a4e9c1a7c4d595fdc40f27c9e8592194d777ee2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1204"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 26</title> <div sID="gen1640" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.1">Le 26:1</reference>, 2. Of Idolatry.<div eID="gen1640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1641" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1204"/><hi type="bold">1. Ye shall make you no idols--</hi>Idolatry had been previously forbidden (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.4">Ex 20:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.20.5">5</reference>), but the law was repeated here with reference to some particular forms of it that were very prevalent among the neighboring nations.<div eID="gen1641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1642" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a standing image--</hi>that is, "upright pillar."<div eID="gen1642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">image of stone--</hi>that is, an obelisk, inscribed with hieroglyphical and superstitious characters; the former denoting the common and smaller pillars of the Syrians or Canaanites; the latter, pointing to the large and elaborate obelisks which the Egyptians worshipped as guardian divinities, or used as stones of adoration to stimulate religious worship. The Israelites were enjoined to beware of them. <div eID="gen1643" type="x-p"/>
entries.a88a689521bf761da7cd706f6e6010407f83e99c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1205"/><div sID="gen1644" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1205"/><hi type="bold">2. Ye shall keep my sabbaths, and reverence my sanctuary--</hi>Very frequently, in this Book of the Law, the Sabbath and the sanctuary are mentioned as antidotes to idolatry. <div eID="gen1644" type="x-p"/>
entries.7775ece406105b20f9cf87fb6008b37161cc9702: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1206"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.26.3-Lev.26.13">Le 26:3-13</reference>. A Blessing to the Obedient.</title> <div sID="gen1645" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1206"/><hi type="bold">3. If ye walk in my statutes--</hi>In that covenant into which God graciously entered with the people of Israel, He promised to bestow upon them a variety of blessings, so long as they continued obedient to Him as their Almighty Ruler; and in their subsequent history that people found every promise amply fulfilled, in the enjoyment of plenty, peace, a populous country, and victory over all enemies. <div eID="gen1645" type="x-p"/>
entries.c372346f9728d997ebb7c497737df025c2991276: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1207"/><div sID="gen1646" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1207"/><hi type="bold">4. I will give you rain in due season, and the land shall yield her increase--</hi>Rain seldom fell in Judea except at two seasons--the former rain at the end of autumn, the seedtime; and the latter rain in spring, before the beginning of harvest (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.24">Jr 5:24</reference>). <div eID="gen1646" type="x-p"/>
entries.d52b4f8c805143813368b70521527a3f2f2e6b62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1208"/><div sID="gen1647" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1208"/><hi type="bold">5. your threshing shall reach unto the vintage, and the vintage shall reach unto the sowing time, &c.--</hi>The barley harvest in Judea was about the middle of April; the wheat harvest about six weeks after, or in the beginning of June. After the harvest came the vintage, and fruit gathering towards the latter end of July. Moses led the Hebrews to believe that, provided they were faithful to God, there would be no idle time between the harvest and vintage, so great would be the increase. (See <reference osisRef="Amos.9.13">Am 9:13</reference>). This promise would be very animating to a people who had come from a country where, for three months, they were pent up without being able to walk abroad because the fields were under water. <div eID="gen1647" type="x-p"/>
entries.e57747f1e181c79c1b4d6c308f3e34de80f676b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1209"/><div sID="gen1648" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1209"/><hi type="bold">10. ye shall eat old store--</hi>Their stock of old corn would be still unexhausted and large when the next harvest brought a new supply. <div eID="gen1648" type="x-p"/>
entries.d3cd1e8ba69a85d0c5a958649f9a288db513047a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1210"/><div sID="gen1649" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1210"/><hi type="bold">13. I have broken the bands of your yoke, and made you go upright--</hi>a metaphorical expression to denote their emancipation from Egyptian slavery. <div eID="gen1649" type="x-p"/>
entries.62e348e5e374e116e2a79543c87ef85a01680a55: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1211"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.26.14-Lev.26.39">Le 26:14-39</reference>. A Curse to the Disobedient.</title> <div sID="gen1650" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1211"/><hi type="bold">14-15. But if ye will not hearken unto me, &c.--</hi>In proportion to the great and manifold privileges bestowed upon the Israelites would be the extent of their national criminality and the severity of their national punishments if they disobeyed. <div eID="gen1650" type="x-p"/>
entries.e8cbac6b85620c8122b06da0f568d29ccfeb24a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1212"/><div sID="gen1651" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1212"/><hi type="bold">16. I will even appoint over you terror--</hi>the falling sickness [Patrick].<div eID="gen1651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1652" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">consumption, and the burning ague--</hi>Some consider these as symptoms of the same disease--consumption followed by the shivering, burning, and sweating fits that are the usual concomitants of that malady. According to the Septuagint, "ague" is "the jaundice," which disorders the eyes and produces great depression of spirits. Others, however, consider the word as referring to a scorching wind; no certain explanation can be given. <div eID="gen1652" type="x-p"/>
entries.110b00ea8a60b1c08b0daf234332a976c56c204d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1213"/><div sID="gen1653" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1213"/><hi type="bold">18. if ye will not yet for all this hearken unto me, then I will punish you seven times more--</hi>that is, with far more severe and protracted calamities. <div eID="gen1653" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a65d7aaa9a73789d1de890b275b4253d1b883d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1214"/><div sID="gen1654" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1214"/><hi type="bold">19. I will make your heaven as iron, and your earth as brass--</hi>No figures could have been employed to convey a better idea of severe and long-continued famine. <div eID="gen1654" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4e4fd5dcfc1a5b8ea0dd3367eda9f69a834d478: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1215"/><div sID="gen1655" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1215"/><hi type="bold">22. I will also send wild beasts among you--</hi>This was one of the four judgments threatened (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.21">Eze 14:21</reference>; see also <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.4">2Ki 2:4</reference>).<div eID="gen1655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1656" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your highways shall be desolate--</hi>Trade and commerce will be destroyed--freedom and safety will be gone--neither stranger nor native will be found on the roads (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.8">Is 33:8</reference>). This is an exact picture of the present state of the Holy Land, which has long lain in a state of desolation, brought on by the sins of the ancient Jews. <div eID="gen1656" type="x-p"/>
entries.19f46ee4102c344e54d19410df1888f5d715693b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1216"/><div sID="gen1657" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1216"/><hi type="bold">26. ten women shall bake your bread in one oven, &c.--</hi>The bread used in families is usually baked by women, and at home. But sometimes also, in times of scarcity, it is baked in public ovens for want of fuel; and the scarcity predicted here would be so great, that one oven would be sufficient to bake as much as ten women used in ordinary occasions to provide for family use; and even this scanty portion of bread would be distributed by weight (<reference osisRef="Ezek.4.16">Eze 4:16</reference>). <div eID="gen1657" type="x-p"/>
entries.702a115fd4333c23652ed76a2924a2fc95ffa56c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1217"/><div sID="gen1658" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1217"/><hi type="bold">29. ye shall eat the flesh of your sons--</hi>The revolting picture was actually exhibited at the siege of Samaria, at the siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.10">La 4:10</reference>), and at the destruction of that city by the Romans. (See on <reference osisRef="Deut.28.53">De 28:53</reference>). <div eID="gen1658" type="x-p"/>
entries.bbc04b6a4b328fe7a2cb23279fbd3b9a54998773: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1218"/><div sID="gen1659" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1218"/><hi type="bold">30. I will destroy your high places--</hi>Consecrated enclosures on the tops of mountains, or on little hillocks, raised for practising the rites of idolatry.<div eID="gen1659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1660" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cut down your images--</hi>According to some, those images were made in the form of chariots (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.11">2Ki 23:11</reference>); according to others, they were of a conical form, like small pyramids. Reared in honor of the sun, they were usually placed on a very high situation, to enable the worshippers to have a better view of the rising sun. They were forbidden to the Israelites, and when set up, ordered to be destroyed.<div eID="gen1660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1661" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast your carcases upon the carcases of your idols, &c.--</hi>Like the statues of idols, which, when broken, lie neglected and contemned, the Jews during the sieges and subsequent captivity often wanted the rites of sepulture. <div eID="gen1661" type="x-p"/>
entries.808290efe192a663115a019447ef49fa364bd60c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1219"/><div sID="gen1662" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1219"/><hi type="bold">31. I will make your cities waste--</hi>This destruction of its numerous and flourishing cities, which was brought upon Judea through the sins of Israel, took place by the forced removal of the people during, and long after, the captivity. But it is realized to a far greater extent now.<div eID="gen1662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1663" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring your sanctuaries unto desolation, and I will not smell the savour of your sweet odours--</hi>the tabernacle and temple, as is evident from the tenor of the subsequent clause, in which God announces that He will not accept or regard their sacrifices. <div eID="gen1663" type="x-p"/>
entries.d141dbc8128da42f14d65fd76b3dcb841e284bcf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1220"/><div sID="gen1664" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1220"/><hi type="bold">33. I will scatter you among the heathen, &c.--</hi>as was done when the elite of the nation were removed into Assyria and placed in various parts of the kingdom. <div eID="gen1664" type="x-p"/>
entries.eebde76a085e647b862fc2f8775493389e851231: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1221"/><div sID="gen1665" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1221"/><hi type="bold">34. Then shall the land enjoy her sabbaths, as long as it lieth desolate, &c.--</hi>A long arrear of sabbatic years had accumulated through the avarice and apostasy of the Israelites, who had deprived their land of its appointed season of rest. The number of those sabbatic years seems to have been seventy, as determined by the duration of the captivity. This early prediction is very remarkable, considering that the usual policy of the Assyrian conquerors was to send colonies to cultivate and inhabit their newly acquired provinces. <div eID="gen1665" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd379ba933b72ca625b073875e00a000823e15e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1222"/><div sID="gen1666" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1222"/><hi type="bold">38. the land of your enemies shall eat you up, &c.--</hi>On the removal of the ten tribes into captivity, they never returned, and all traces of them were lost. <div eID="gen1666" type="x-p"/>
entries.eeb47c4c68e756204e2085e1792eadcdccf33fce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1223"/><div sID="gen1667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1223"/><hi type="bold">40-45. If they shall confess their iniquity, &c.--</hi>This passage holds out the gracious promise of divine forgiveness and favor on their repentance, and their happy restoration to their land, in memory of the covenant made with their fathers (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.1-Rom.2.29">Ro 2:1-29</reference>). <div eID="gen1667" type="x-p"/>
entries.31046ec035037aa4eaed4110f4f64abb17bfbe5f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1224"/><div sID="gen1668" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1224"/><hi type="bold">46. These are the statutes and judgments and laws--</hi>It has been thought by some that the last chapter was originally placed after the twenty-fifth [Adam Clarke], while others consider that the next chapter was added as an appendix, in consequence of many people being influenced by the promises and threats of the preceding one, to resolve that they would dedicate themselves and their possessions to the service of God [Calmet]. <chapter eID="Lev.26"/>

entries.4c74e5f0c1dd229688713f3f909e8c4ade0a69e6: <div eID="gen5043" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen5044" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5045" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5045" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5044" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5046" type="x-p"/> Idolatry forbidden, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.1">Lev 26:1</reference>. The Sabbath to be sanctified, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.2-Lev.26.3">Lev 26:2-3</reference>. Promises to obedience, of fruitful fields, plentiful harvests, and vintage, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.4-Lev.26.5">Lev 26:4-5</reference>. Of peace and security, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.6">Lev 26:6</reference>. Discomfiture of their enemies, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.7-Lev.26.9">Lev 26:7-9</reference>. Of abundance, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.10">Lev 26:10</reference>. Of the divine presence, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.11-Lev.26.13">Lev 26:11-13</reference>. Threatenings against the disobedient, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.14-Lev.26.15">Lev 26:14-15</reference>. Of terror and dismay, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.16">Lev 26:16</reference>. Their enemies shall prevail against them, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.17-Lev.26.18">Lev 26:17-18</reference>. Of barrenness, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.19-Lev.26.20">Lev 26:19-20</reference>. Of desolation by wild beasts, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.21-Lev.26.22">Lev 26:21-22</reference>. And if not humbled and reformed, worse evils shall be inflicted upon them, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.23-Lev.26.24">Lev 26:23-24</reference>. Their enemies shall prevail, and they shall be wasted by the pestilence, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.25-Lev.26.26">Lev 26:25-26</reference>. If they should still continue refractory, they shall be yet more sorely punished, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.27-Lev.26.28">Lev 26:27-28</reference>. The famine shall so increase that they shall be obliged to eat their own children, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.29">Lev 26:29</reference>. Their carcasses shall be cast upon the carcasses of their idols, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Lev 26:30</reference>. Their cities shall be wasted, and the sanctuary desolated, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.31">Lev 26:31</reference>; the land destroyed, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.32">Lev 26:32</reference>; themselves scattered among their enemies, and pursued with utter confusion and distress, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.33-Lev.26.39">Lev 26:33-39</reference>. If under these judgments they confess their sin and return to God, He will remember them in mercy, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.40-Lev.26.43">Lev 26:40-43</reference>; visit them even in the land of their enemies, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.44">Lev 26:44</reference>; and remember His covenant with their fathers, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.45">Lev 26:45</reference>. The conclusion, stating these to be the judgments and laws which the Lord made between himself and the children of Israel in Mount Sinai, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.46">Lev 26:46</reference>. <div eID="gen5046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5047" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen5047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5048" type="x-p"/> Ye shall make you no idols - See note on <reference osisRef="Exo.20.4">Exo 20:4</reference>, and see the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.28.18-Gen.28.19">Gen 28:18-19</reference> (note), concerning consecrated stones. Not only idolatry in general is forbidden here, but also the superstitious use of innocent and lawful things. Probably the stones or pillars which were first set up, and anointed by holy men in commemoration of signal interposition of God in their behalf, were afterward abused to idolatrous and superstitious purposes, and therefore prohibited. This we know was the case with the brazen serpent, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.4">2Kgs 18:4</reference>.
entries.c05c062cf88dd54d260e75f21236714dd50b8272: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen5048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5049" type="x-p"/> If ye walk in my statutes - For the meaning of this and similar words used in the law, See the note on <reference osisRef="Lev.26.15">Lev 26:15</reference>.
entries.ad92bd436fc2ad41dc5c9d5edc5a6fe596406e21: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen5049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5050" type="x-p"/> Rain in due season - What in Scripture is called the early and the latter rain. The first fell in Palestine at the commencement of spring, and the latter in autumn - Calmet.
entries.745ae1dcd110ae29ae756f836957777112ffa6ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen5050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5051" type="x-p"/> Your threshing shall reach unto the vintage - According to Pliny, Hist. Nat., l. xviii., c. 18, the Egyptians reaped their barley six months, and their oats seven months, after seed time; for they sowed all their grain about the end of summer, when the overflowings of the Nile had ceased. It was nearly the same in Judaea: they sowed their corn and barley towards the end of autumn, and about the month of October; and they began their barley-harvest after the passover, about the middle of March; and in one month or six weeks after, about pentecost, they began that of their wheat. After their wheat-harvest their vintage commenced. Moses here leads the Hebrews to hope, if they continued faithful to God, that between their harvest and vintage, and between their vintage and seed-time, there should be no interval, so great should the abundance be; and these promises would appear to them the more impressive, as they had just now come out of a country where the inhabitants were obliged to remain for nearly three months shut up within their cities, because the Nile had then inundated the whole country. See Calmet. "This is a nervous and beautiful promise of such entire plenty of corn and wine, that before they could have reaped and threshed out their corn the vintage should be ready, and before they could have pressed out their wine it would be time to sow again. The Prophet Amos, <reference osisRef="Amo.9.13">Amo 9:13</reference> expresses the same blessing in the same manner: The ploughman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes him who soweth seed." - Dodd.
entries.12fefee57c91d94f7f8f33442caeeb815238dc05: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen5051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5052" type="x-p"/> I will set my tabernacle among you - This and the following verse contain the grand promise of the Gospel dispensation, viz. the presence, manifestation, and indwelling of God in human nature, and his constant in dwelling in the souls of his followers. So <reference osisRef="Joh.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference> the Word was made flesh, και εσκηνωσεν εν ἡμιν, and Made His Tabernacle among us. And to this promise of the law St. Paul evidently refers, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.16-2Cor.6.18">2Cor 6:16-18</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.1">2Cor 7:1</reference>
entries.8254d57d696865b43b062c069b22244784b30ffd: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen5052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5053" type="x-p"/> If ye shall despise my statutes - abhor my judgments - As these words, and others of a similar import, which point out different properties of the revelation of God, are frequently occurring, I Judge it best to take a general view of them, once for all, in this place, and show how they differ among themselves, and what property of the Divine law each points out. <div eID="gen5053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5054" type="x-p"/> 1. Statutes. חקת chukkoth, from חק chak, to mark out, define, etc. This term seems to signify the things which God has defined, marked, and traced out, that men might have a perfect copy of pure conduct always before their eyes, to teach them how they might walk so as to please him in all things, which they could not do without such instruction as God gives in his word, and the help which he affords by his Spirit. <div eID="gen5054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5055" type="x-p"/> 2. Judgments. שפטים shephatim, from שפט shaphat, to distinguish, regulate, and determine; meaning those things which God has determined that men shall pursue, by which their whole conduct shall be regulated, making the proper distinction between virtue and vice, good and evil, right and wrong, justice and injustice; in a word, between what is proper to be done, and what is proper to be left undone. <div eID="gen5055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5056" type="x-p"/> 3. Commandments. מצות mitsvoth, from צוה tsavah, to command, ordain, and appoint, as a legislator. This term is properly applied to those parts of the law which contain the obligation the people are under to act according to the statutes, judgments, etc., already established, and which prohibit them by penal sanctions from acting contrary to the laws. <div eID="gen5056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5057" type="x-p"/> 4. Covenant. ברית berith, from בר bar, to clear, cleanse, or purify; because the covenant, the whole system of revelation given to the Jews, was intended to separate them from all the people of the earth, and to make them holy. Berith also signifies the covenant-sacrifice, which prefigured the atonement made by Christ for the sin of the world, by which he purifies believers unto himself, and makes them a peculiar people, zealous of good works. Besides those four, we may add the following, from other places of Scripture. <div eID="gen5057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5058" type="x-p"/> 5. Testimonies. עדות edoth, from עד ad, beyond, farther, besides; because the whole ritual law referred to something farther on or beyond the Jewish dispensation, even to that sacrifice which in the fullness of time was to be offered for the sins of men. Thus all the sacrifices, etc., of the Mosaic law referred to Christ, and bore testimony to him who was to come. <div eID="gen5058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5059" type="x-p"/> 6. Ordinances. משמרות mishmaroth, from שמר shamar, to guard, keep safe, watch over; those parts of Divine revelation which exhorted men to watch their ways, keep their hearts, and promised them, in consequence, the continual protection and blessing of God their Maker. <div eID="gen5059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5060" type="x-p"/> 7. Precepts. פקודים pikkudim, from פקד pakad, to overlook, take care or notice of, to visit; a very expressive character of the Divine testimonies, the overseers of a man's conduct, those who stand by and look on to see whether he acts according to the commands of his Master; also the visitors, because God's precepts are suited to all the circumstances of human life; some are applicable in adversity, others in prosperity; some in times of temptation and sadness, others in seasons of spiritual joy and exultation, etc., etc. Thus they may be said to overlook and visit man in all times, places, and circumstances. <div eID="gen5060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5061" type="x-p"/> 8. Truth. אמת emeth, from אם am, to support, sustain, confirm; because God is immutable who has promised, threatened, commanded, and therefore all his promises, threatenings, commandments, etc., are unalterable and eternal. Error and falsity promise to direct and sustain, but they fail. God's word is supported by his own faithfulness, and it supports and confirms them who conscientiously believe it. <div eID="gen5061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5062" type="x-p"/> 9. Righteousness. צדקה tsedakah, from צדק which, though not used as a verb in the Hebrew Bible, seems to convey, from its use as a noun, the idea of giving just weight or good measure, see <reference osisRef="Lev.19.36">Lev 19:36</reference>. This is one of the characters which is attributed to the revelation God makes of himself; (see <reference osisRef="Psa.119.137-Psa.119.144">Psa 119:137-144</reference>); and by this the impartiality of the Divine testimonies is pointed out. God gives to all their due, and his word distributes to every man according to his state, circumstances, talents, graces, etc.; to none too much, to none too little, to all enough. <div eID="gen5062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5063" type="x-p"/> 10. Word Of Jehovah. דבר יהוה debar Yehovah, from דבר, dabar, to drive, lead, bring forward, hence to bring forward, or utter one's sentiments; so the word of God is what God has brought forth to man from his own mind and counsel; it is a perfect similitude of his own righteousness, holiness, goodness, and truth. This Divine law is sometimes expressed by: - <div eID="gen5063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5064" type="x-p"/> 11. אמרה imrah, speech or word, variously modified from אמר amar, to branch out, because of the interesting details into which the word of God enters in order to instruct man and make him wise unto salvation, or, as the apostle expresses it, "God, who at sundry times, and in divers manners, spake unto the fathers by the prophets," πολυμερως και πολυτροπως, in many distinct parcels, and by various tropes or figures; a curious and elegant description of Divine revelation; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.1">Heb 1:1</reference>. <div eID="gen5064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5065" type="x-p"/> 12. All these collectively are termed the Law תורה torah, or תורת יהוה torath Yehovah, the law of the Lord, from ירה yarah, to direct, set straight and true, as stones in a building, to teach and instruct, because this whole system of Divine revelation is calculated to direct men to the attainment of present and eternal felicity, to set them right in their notions concerning the supreme God, to order and adjust them in the several departments of civil and religious society, and thus to teach and instruct them in the knowledge of themselves, and in the true knowledge of God. Thus those who receive the truth become the city of the living God - the temple of the Most High, built together for a habitation of God through the Spirit. To complete this description of the word law, See the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.12.49">Exo 12:49</reference>, where other properties of the law of God are specified.
entries.1246b13fed6a25a3e662fd69b045cdbe67f608a3: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen5065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5066" type="x-p"/> I will even appoint over you terror, etc. - How dreadful is this curse! A whole train of evils are here personified and appointed to be the governors of a disobedient people. Terror is to be one of their keepers. How awful a state! to be continually under the influence of dismay, feeling indescribable evils, and fearing worse! Consumption, שחפת shachepheth, generally allowed to be some kind of atrophy or marasmus, by which the flesh was consumed, and the whole body dried up by raging fever through lack of sustenance. See the note on <reference osisRef="Lev.11.16">Lev 11:16</reference>. How circumstantially were all these threatenings fulfilled in this disobedient and rebellious people! Let a deist read over this chapter and compare it with the state of the Jews since the days of Vespasian, and then let him doubt the authenticity of this word if he can.
entries.bc3884405c2dbeaef86fbdbf460fd986263facd3: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen5066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5067" type="x-p"/> I will also send wild beasts among you - God fulfilled these threatenings at different times. He sent fiery Serpents among them, <reference osisRef="Num.21.6">Num 21:6</reference>; Lions, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.25">2Kgs 17:25</reference>; Bears, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.24">2Kgs 2:24</reference>, and threatened them with total desolation, so that their land should be overrun with wild beasts, etc., see <reference osisRef="Eze.5.17">Eze 5:17</reference>. "Spiritually," says Mr. Ainsworth, "these are wicked rulers and tyrants that kill and spoil, <reference osisRef="Pro.28.15">Pro 28:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.3-Dan.7.6">Dan 7:3-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.80.13">Psa 80:13</reference>; and false prophets that devour souls, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.15">Mat 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.1">Rev 13:1</reference>, etc. So the prophet, speaking of their punishment by tyrants, says: A Lion out of the forest shall slay them; a Wolf of the evening shall spoil them; a Leopard shall watch over their cities; every one that goeth out thence shall be torn to pieces, because their transgressions be many. And of their prophets it is said: O Israel, thy prophets are like Foxes in the deserts, <reference osisRef="Eze.13.4">Eze 13:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.8.17">Jer 8:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.15.3">Jer 15:3</reference>."
entries.08798e830b6825d33b9795f4c70d43314e3f744a: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen5067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5068" type="x-p"/> Ten women shall bake your bread in one oven - Though in general every family in the East bakes its own bread, yet there are some public bakehouses where the bread of several families is baked at a certain price.
